newsitem.title: USA: Atlanta mayor eyes privatizing water system - paper.
newsitem.headline: Atlanta mayor eyes privatizing water system - paper.

text.p: Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell will announce plans Friday to privatize operations of the city's water and sewer systems and use the proceeds to fund extensive repairs to the system, the Atlanta Journal Constitution said Friday.
First, the mayor will propose that the city immediately sell $180 million of bonds to cover state fines and improve pollution control measures, the newspaper said.
Atlanta now pays $7.2 million a year in state fines because its sewer system, which empties into the Chattahoochee River, does not meet anti-pollution standards.

Aides said Campbell hoped to have private managers in place by the end of this election year. The mayor told the newspaper he had already solicited three unidentified engineering companies for ideas on how to convert the trouble-prone system to private management.

Campbell said privatization would negate most of the 81 percent, four-year sewer rate increase he proposed last month. He said that would be reduced to a one-year, 14-percent increase and that a proposed increase in water bills for commercial users would be dropped.
"The increase is onerous," the newspaper quoted Campbell as saying. "We do not want to hurt the poor or seniors, nor do we want to curtail economic development."
The sudden change in plans became possible last month when the Internal Revenue Service revised rules limiting the private operation of public facilities that use tax-exempt bonds.
The revisions allow local governments to contract management services for up to 20 years, instead of the current maximum of five years.
Byron Marshall, the mayor's top aide, estimated that private management could save the city $20 million a year over 20 years.
Much of Atlanta's water system is almost 100 years old, and the city plans to replace nearly 3 million feet of aging water lines.

Under Campbell's plan, leasing the water-sewer system would bring in $400 million over the 20-year period, enough to pay for most of the needed anti-pollution upgrades and a revamping of the water system.
Presumably, the newspaper said, the management company would have access to some money generated by the system, which was $132 million in 1995.
Campbell has talked to union leaders who view the plan with suspicion, the newspaper said.
"We want to make sure whatever goes down the pike isn't detrimental to our employees," said Lewis Peeples, spokesman for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees.
Many local governments have privatized management of water or sewer operations, said Bob Rivers, the former head of the city water system.
"This is a very common practice. This is not a first-time thing," Rivers said.
